 Behemoth! 
 By Brian Eggert | November 17, 2026 
 Stanley Kubrick famously said that movies should be more like music than fiction, with shifting moods and feelings, not the linearity of traditional storytelling. Kubrick meant that movies should reflect life, which is shaped like music, not a narrative; it ebbs and flows in unpredictable ways, refusing to conform to our plans. Tony Gilroy took that to heart while writing and directing Behemoth! , a film about a skilled cellist played by Pedro Pascal, who, in one scene, asks a young colleague, “Train or river?” He wants to know whether she’s merely performing the notes on the page or giving them life and feeling. It’s part of a philosophy, similar to Kubrick’s statement, that explains the film’s meandering structure. Behemoth! portrays artistic revelation, devastating loss, and potential parenthood, with a tone that ranges from melodrama to sitcom-worthy farce. And while Kubrick’s observation may be true of life and an aspirational goal for cinema, only the rare master can capture this unpredictable flow onscreen and make the outcome feel cohesive.
 Tony Gilroy’s Behemoth! opens theatrically on December 4.  The full review is exclusive to Patreon subscribers until then. To read it, you can purchase individual access   or join Deep Focus Review’s Patron community .
